1.pericope_label: The kings league together, and Gibeon takes another road

schools.summary: Calvin judges that the kings' minds were intoxicated from above with security, calls it excessive stupor not to have stood on guard until two towns were sacked, and reads God's sparing of his people's weakness in the delay; on the ruse he grants that the Gibeonites judged prudently in bearing anything rather than provoke God further, but condemns the fraud as absurd and inequitable, asks what stability a league so founded could have, blames Joshua and the rulers for bargaining rashly about an uninvestigated matter, and lays down that Joshua was contracting with mere masks and bound only according to the words used. Gill notes that no king of Gibeon is mentioned and infers a government of elders, while reporting an Arabic writer who has a king of Gibeon petition Joshua with gifts and be restored to his throne.

Henry finds the delay strange twice over, that the kings did not act sooner when Israel's design was no secret, and that they acted now when Jericho and Ai should have counselled peace; he attributes it to presumption or despair and observes that many do not know the things belonging to their peace until they are hidden from their eyes. On Gibeon he makes the contrast the point, that the same news irritated others into war and drew these into peace, as the gospel is to some a savour of life and to others of death and the same sun softens wax and hardens clay; he infers from the absence of any king that elders governed, a single ruler being likely too high-hearted to yield.

Clarke takes Gibeon for the capital of the Hivites and traces its later allotment to Benjamin and assignment to the priests. Wesley turns the confederacy into a reproach, wishing that Israel would learn from Canaanites who were often at variance among themselves and yet sacrificed private interests to unite against a common enemy.

Keil sets out the sequence, that Gibeon moved before the league was formed and succeeded because Joshua and the elders fell into the snare without inquiring of the Lord, and quotes the judgment that the account warns the Church of every age against a world seeking peaceable recognition from the kingdom of God; he calls Gibeon one of the royal cities, larger than Ai and held by brave Hivites, traces its allotment to Benjamin, its Levitical status and its housing of the tabernacle from the destruction of Nob until Solomon's temple, and identifies the site by ancient distance and with a village two hours north-west of Jerusalem. Ellicott notes that Gibeon was one member of a group of four cities, and sees a curious compensation in the stratagem, since a stratagem had once destroyed a single Hivite city and now saves four.

debates: Whether Gibeon was a royal city: Keil counts it among them, while Gill and Henry both observe that no king of Gibeon is ever named and infer a government of elders, Gill nevertheless reporting an Arabic tradition of a king who petitioned Joshua and was restored
outliers: Ellicott sees the deception as a curious compensation for Shechem, where a stratagem destroyed one Hivite city and here saves four
Gill reports an Arabic writer according to whom the king of Gibeon wrote to Joshua, sent him large gifts, was kept safe and set again on his throne
Keil quotes the remark that this history is a standing warning to the Church against the cunning of a world seeking peaceable recognition from the kingdom of God
Calvin holds that because the Gibeonites presented themselves under a false character Joshua contracted no obligation beyond the words they had used

4.pericope_label: The disguise, the request for a league, and the artful answers

schools.summary: Calvin argues that in strict law the covenant was null, since all that was stipulated was safety for a people coming from a remote region, and every repetition of the falsehood further annuls a compact drawn out by fraud, the Israelites having expressly excluded the inhabitants of the land; nothing could therefore be gained by the fraud, nor were the Gibeonites helped by the fallacious use of the divine name. Gill notices the emphatic 'also' dropped by the version and offers three comparisons for the craft, with the other nations, with Israel at Ai and, from a rabbinic source, with Simeon and Levi at Shechem, whose Hivite victims were of the same people; he also records the offer to be servants to Joshua alone rather than to the whole people, and their care to magnify the distance while naming no country.

Clarke finds it strange that the Israelites suspected as much as they did and stranger that they took so little care; he allows that stratagems in war are held legal by the practice of all nations while refusing to defend the lies, holds that plain submission would have served the Gibeonites better since lying always defeats its own purpose, works over the words for the mouldy bread and the mended shoes, infers from the verb for making a league that heathenism then had its own covenant sacrifices, and reads the interview as an artful mixture of truth, falsehood and hypocrisy addressed to the commander rather than to the elders. Wesley finds the general submission itself ground for Joshua's suspicion.

Ellicott explains why the disguise was not detected, since a people whose raiment had not waxed old in forty years and who lived on manna had no experience of worn garments or stale provisions; he reports that the verb for making themselves ambassadors occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible and that a one-letter change in the Greek and Aramaic versions turns it into taking provision, and hears in the Israelites' question the assumption that Canaan was already their own. Keil remarks that the envoys say nothing of the crossing of the Jordan or the fall of Jericho, and quotes the reason, that men from a very distant land could not yet have heard by report of things so lately done.

debates: Whether the stratagem should have been detected: Clarke twice calls the Israelites incautious, finding it strange that they suspected what they did and then acted on the suspicion so little, while Ellicott argues that people whose own clothes and shoes had not worn out in forty years had no experience by which to judge worn garments and stale bread

How the fraud stands in law: Clarke allows that stratagems in war are reckoned legal by all nations while denying that the lying is commended or exemplary, whereas Calvin holds the covenant null in strict law because its terms covered only a distant people
outliers: Gill records a rabbinic reading by which the Hivites are named from the serpent and the Gibeonites so called because they deceived Israel as the serpent deceived Eve
Ellicott reports that the verb for playing the ambassador is found nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, and that the ancient versions read it, by one letter's difference, as taking provision
Clarke infers from the idiom for making a league, to cut a covenant sacrifice, that the heathen of that date ratified covenants by sacrificing to their gods and invoking them

10.pericope_label: The victuals examined, the Lord not consulted, and the league sworn

schools.summary: Gill takes the princes to have handled rather than eaten the bread, citing rabbinic authorities for whom its dryness was the convincing evidence, and argues against the covenant-meal reading on the ground that better fare would have been provided. Calvin dismisses both the tasting and the covenant feast as insipid fictions, reads the clause as an indirect censure of a credulity that fastened on the bread without noticing how little colour the story had, and supplies the geography that makes the credulity indefensible, the Gibeonite capital standing some fourteen miles from Jericho and half that from Ai.

Henry turns the neglect of inquiry into a proverb, that we make more haste than good speed when we do not stay to take God with us, and notes that the fraud was soon found out, a lying tongue being but for a moment. He describes the treaty as quickly and informally made, with life the only thing asked and a great favour in the wars of Canaan, and observes that Joshua acted with the princes rather than alone, treating them as sharers in a government to which he had an extraordinary call. On the binding force he states principle and limit together, that an unlawful oath would not have bound since no obligation can make it a duty to sin, but that sparing Canaanites who submitted and left idolatry was not unlawful, and a citizen of Zion swears to his own hurt and changes not; and he notes that the princes neither sought release from the high priest nor pleaded that no faith need be kept.

Clarke supposes an actual meal taken in friendship, eating together being in those countries a token of unalterable friendship so that those who share even salt reckon themselves in perpetual covenant, while allowing that the marginal reading should not be hastily rejected; he calls the failure to inquire highly reprehensible because the interest and honour of God as king were concerned in a state transaction, and infers from the wording that the covenant was made in the ordinary manner with a sacrifice whose blood was poured out before the Lord. Wesley draws the rule that God should be consulted in every business of importance, concedes that he would probably have consented to sparing the Gibeonites though with more caution and an obligation to embrace the true religion, and gives three reasons for holding the league binding.

Keil names the neglected means of inquiry and the substitute accepted, as though dry mouldy bread were a safe guarantee of truth; he observes that letting them live is the only article recorded, both as the main point and because Canaanites ought properly to have been destroyed, and denies that any express command was broken, since the law forbade treaties with Canaanites, which these were not supposed to be. Ellicott changes the subject of the clause about the victuals, following the margin and the Aramaic version so that the princes accepted the men on the strength of their provisions, 'the men' meaning the envoys.

debates: What the princes did with the provisions: Gill has them handle and inspect the bread, Clarke supposes a meal of friendship amounting to a perpetual covenant, Ellicott follows the margin and the Aramaic so that they accepted the men on the strength of the provisions, and Calvin rejects both tasting and covenant feast as insipid fictions in favour of a censure of credulity

Whether the sworn league bound Israel: Keil argues no express command was broken, Wesley gives three reasons for its validity, and Henry allows that an unlawful oath would not have bound while holding this one lawful, all of which stands against Calvin's earlier position that a compact obtained by fraud is null in strict law
outliers: Calvin fixes the distance of the Gibeonite capital at some fourteen miles from Jericho and half that from Ai, where Israel had lately been fighting
Clarke reports that in those countries men who have eaten even salt together reckon themselves bound in a perpetual covenant
Wesley infers from the statement that God hardened the other cities against seeking peace that their destruction followed their own obstinacy rather than a peremptory command
Henry observes that Joshua, for all his extraordinary call to the government, treated the princes as sharers in it rather than keeping them in the dark or under foot

16.pericope_label: The fraud discovered, the congregation murmurs, and the oath holds

schools.summary: Calvin treats the swift discovery as a chastisement of their levity that sharpened the shame, since sloth had made them stumble over a matter almost set before their eyes, and sees a paternal indulgence in their quiet passage through the region, God turning to their good what might justly have hurt them; on the oath he poses two questions formally, whether men who never meant to pledge faith to impostors contracted any obligation and whether the people might rescind what their leaders foolishly promised, and answers that the obligation of an oath is to be held in the greatest sacredness, so that we may not resile on the plea of error even from pacts in which we were deceived, God's name being more precious than the wealth of a whole world. Gill dates the treaty to the very day the envoys arrived, notes their haste and Israel's want of inquiry, and records that the report was found true and the deception established without a blow struck.

Clarke measures the distance from the camp to show that three days were ample to expose the fraud, infers from the ark's later residence at one of the towns that the preservation of the Gibeonites did not displease the Lord, ascribes the murmuring to a predatory spirit robbed of its spoils and notes that God at times interdicted such spoils altogether; on the oath he concedes that the engagement was vitiated and void on the part of the deceived, yet holds that the sacrifice and the swearing by the divine name bound them as to life, and argues from Joshua's never being reprehended and from the later punishment of a king who thought himself loosed. Wesley gives two causes for the murmuring, the desire of spoil and the proneness of a people to censure its rulers.

Keil records the march to the four towns and their arrival on the third day and gives the princes' reason for not striking, that they might not touch them because of their oath lest wrath come upon them. Ellicott divides the four towns between Benjamin and Judah and finds in that division the explanation of a later king's attempt to confiscate Gibeonite land for his followers, notes that Gibeon became a city of the priests and the seat of the tabernacle while another of the towns held the ark, and holds that a covenant made in the name of the Lord is his and cannot be broken however it was obtained, adding that the law had raised the tone of morality here beyond that of many Christians.

debates: Why an oath obtained by fraud binds: Clarke concedes the engagement was vitiated and void on the part of the deceived yet holds the swearing by the divine name binding as to life, Ellicott holds simply that a covenant made in God's name is his and cannot be broken, and Calvin, having called the compact null in strict law, answers his own two questions by the sacredness of an oath, from which no plea of error permits a man to resile
outliers: Ellicott remarks that the law of the Lord had raised the tone of morality in this particular beyond that of many Christians, who would not hesitate to repudiate an agreement concluded under false pretences
Clarke ascribes the congregation's murmuring to a predatory spirit deprived of plunder, and holds that God interdicted the spoils of certain conquered cities because he saw that proneness
The Calvin block carries an editorial note marking the appearance of inconsistency between his verdict that the compact was null in strict law and his insistence that the oath must be kept

20.pericope_label: The middle course, the service imposed, and Joshua’s reproof

schools.summary: Calvin calls the settlement a partial ratification, since men entitled to perfect security are stripped of a liberty dearer than life, and infers that Joshua and the rest devised a middle course in perplexity so as not to make the oath void, the chief object being to appease the multitude while still punishing the fraud; he does not soften the terms, noting the removal from home to a wandering life and the meanness of the labour, and he defends the justice of the sentence on the ground that nothing would be more unbecoming than to let wiles profit those who use them, so that the blame falls back on men cursed by their own act. Gill hears the same doubleness in the princes' phrase, which may name either the sparing of life or the punishment not yet spoken, and notes how importunate they were about the lives because of the oath.

Henry supposes that the elders of Gibeon and its dependent cities, not the original messengers, were now treated with so that the matter might be fully compromised, and dwells on the mildness of the reproof, Joshua loading them with no ill names and not calling them, as they deserved, base liars, but only asking why they had beguiled him; from which he draws the lesson that under the greatest provocation it is our wisdom and duty to keep our temper, since a just cause needs no anger to defend it and a bad one is never the better for it. He also states the best excuse the case would bear, that they found a sentence of death passed on them in the word of God and no opposing it in his works, and so resolved to try his mercy.

Clarke suspects that hewing wood and drawing water is a proverbial expression for the lowest state of servitude, while allowing that it may be meant literally. Wesley takes it literally and divides it, one kind of drudgery standing for the rest, so that they were public servants partly for the sacrifices and services of God's house which Israel would otherwise have performed, partly for the camp, and sometimes for particular Israelites; he agrees that the elders themselves were probably now present.

Keil reads the sentence as a curse of perpetual servitude, the idiom meaning that a servant shall never be cut off from among them, takes the definition of the service to be labour for the house of God which the law assigns to the lowest classes of the people, and connects the whole arrangement with the ancient curse pronounced upon Canaan.

debates: Whether hewing wood and drawing water is literal or proverbial: Clarke suspects a proverbial phrase for the lowest servitude while allowing the literal sense, whereas Wesley and Keil both take it of actual labour, Wesley dividing it between the sanctuary, the camp and private Israelites and Keil confining the definition to the house of God
outliers: Calvin holds that the covenant was ratified only in part, since the Gibeonites were entitled to perfect security and were instead deprived of a liberty dearer than life
Calvin also notes the harshness of assigning no term to the servitude, the words meaning that slaves shall never cease from among them
Keil connects the sentence with the ancient curse pronounced upon Canaan
Henry draws from the mildness of the reproof the rule that a just cause needs no anger to defend it, and a bad one is never the better for it

23.pericope_label: The curse of Canaan, the question of the Nethinim, and the sentence executed

schools.summary: Gill takes the Gibeonites to be shown as the posterity of cursed Canaan whom their artifice could not exempt, finds the old words fulfilled in their serving the Levites and the seed of Shem, and suggests they were spared in providence so that this part of the curse might stand; but he alone turns the sentence round, since the mean office gave them a place in the sanctuary and the opportunity of learning God's law and true worship, so that the curse became a blessing and they stand as an emblem and pledge of the reception of the Gentiles into the church. He also reports the derivation of the name Nethinim from the verb by which Joshua gave them to the sanctuary.

Clarke holds that the curse of Ham implied slavery and nothing else and that nothing but perpetual slavery is implied here, describing a people put under tribute, set to the meanest offices, stripped of national importance and never allowed to incorporate with Israel, and comparing them to a servile caste he had met with elsewhere; he supposes God's purpose towards all the Canaanite nations to have been extirpation for those who kept their idolatry and tributary slavery for those who renounced it, denies that the Gibeonites can be identified with the Nethinim for want of decisive proof, makes self-preservation the motive of their fraud, admires their surrender as an appeal full of delicacy and cogent argument, and distributes the outcome exactly between mercy in the deliverance and justice in the labour. Wesley reads the sentence as a change in the quality of the curse rather than an escape from it, entailed on their posterity, identifies them with the Nethinim of the temple service, and turns their submission into a prayer to submit likewise to Christ.

Keil states the excuse simply, that having heard of the command given through Moses they feared for their lives and readily submitted, and closes on a point of dating, that the clause about the place God would choose sentences them to serve at the altar wherever the sanctuary should stand rather than sending them at once, and that while 'unto this day' shows the account was written after the event, the future tense shows it was written before the choice was made. Ellicott supports the identification with the Nethinim from the enumeration of the returned captives and the coupling of Solomon's servants with them, observes that the precedent seems to have been followed by Solomon with the remnant of the doomed nations, and infers that the existence of so large a body of Canaanites shows the sentence on the seven nations was not executed on the mass of the non-resisting population.

debates: Whether the Gibeonites are the Nethinim of the later books: Wesley identifies them outright and derives the name from their gift to the sanctuary, Gill reports the same derivation and Ellicott supports it from the lists of returned captives, while Clarke denies any decisive proof and thinks the Nethinim were slaves of a different race, the Gibeonites having been nearly annihilated by Saul

How the curse is to be understood: Clarke restricts it to perpetual slavery and makes it the pattern of God's purpose for all Canaanites who renounced idolatry, and Wesley calls it a change in the quality of the curse rather than an escape, while Gill holds that for these people the curse was turned into a blessing by their place in the sanctuary
outliers: Gill reads the Gibeonites' place in the sanctuary as an emblem and pledge of the reception of the Gentiles into the church of God
Ellicott argues that the survival of so large a body of Canaanites shows the sentence of destruction on the seven nations was not executed on the mass of the non-resisting population
Keil dates the composition of the account between the event and the choosing of the sanctuary's place, from the phrase 'unto this day' on one side and the future tense on the other
